original.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
original.key_identity: Gaussian case: P(sqrt n s_n <= t) = 1 - exp(-t^2/2 - t), so the conjectured constant is the Gaussian value.
original.method: Test whether the constant 1 in front of t is forced by the Gaussian comparison and whether the Bernoulli case can beat it.
original.obstruction: Hard-edge universality covers t >= n^{-c}; the conjecture needs the constant 1 down to exponentially small t.
original.result: For the Gaussian matrix Edelman's exact law gives P(sqrt n s_n <= t) = 1 - e^{-t^2/2 - t} ~ t as t -> 0, so the constant 1 is exactly the Gaussian density at zero of sqrt n s_n; the conjecture says Bernoulli matrices are no worse than Gaussian up to the exponentially small singular mass. A sufficient condition would be a local limit theorem for sqrt n s_n at zero uniform in n, which is a universality statement at the hard edge (the smallest singular value) and is known (Tao-Vu 2010 hard-edge universality) only in the form P(sqrt n s_n <= t) = (1 - e^{-t^2/2-t}) + O(n^{-c}) for t in a fixed range, which gives the conjecture for t >= n^{-c'} but not for t between c^n and n^{-c'}. The gap regime is exactly the small-ball regime where the Rudelson-Vershynin constant C appears. No improvement obtained.

corrected_draft.key_identity: Real Gaussian hard-edge LIMIT: for each fixed t>=0, P(sqrt(n) s_min(G_n)<=t)=1-exp(-t-t^2/2)+o(1) as n tends to infinity. This is not an exact finite-n identity.
corrected_draft.method: Test whether the constant 1 in front of t is forced by the Gaussian comparison and whether the Bernoulli case can beat it.
corrected_draft.obstruction: Hard-edge universality covers t >= n^{-c}; the conjecture needs the constant 1 down to exponentially small t.
corrected_draft.result: The limiting real-Gaussian law has slope one at zero. At finite n=1 the CDF is erf(t/sqrt(2)), with slope sqrt(2/pi). Tao--Vu Theorem 1.1 gives the real formula with an o(1) error, and Theorem 1.3 gives a uniform polynomial error under its moment hypotheses. Sah--Sahasrabudhe--Sawhney Theorem 1.1 supplies coefficient 1+O((log n)^(-1/16)) and an exponential remainder, rather than the exact coefficient one. The original exact-coefficient route remains incomplete; no improvement or solved claim is inferred.
